Recent Fixes and Field-List Corrections

Source: vignettes/articles/recent-fixes.Rmd
recent-fixes.Rmd

Why this exists

This fork (einarhjorleifsson/icesDatras) tracks ices-tools-prod/icesDatras closely – as of writing, one commit ahead of upstream master. While using the package as a dependency of another project (obus), several real, reproducible bugs surfaced. This article documents what was found, what was fixed, why – and, just as importantly, one thing that looked like a bug but wasn’t.

Everything here lives on einar_dev/integration in this fork, not yet on master and not yet proposed upstream. It’s written up both as a personal reference and as a starting point should it be worth raising with the people maintaining the upstream repository.

A three-way distinction that shaped what got “fixed” here

Not every wrong-looking result is fixable the same way:

  • Code bug – given the same values the DATRAS API already returns, a function’s own logic produces a result that contradicts a clear, well-defined convention. Fixable permanently in this package’s own R source.
  • Data bug – the values themselves, as submitted to DATRAS, are wrong or inconsistent regardless of what any client code does with them. Not fixable here at all.
  • Webserver/schema gap – ICES’s own field-list webservice (getDatrasFieldList()) is missing or wrong, even though the underlying survey data is fine. Fixable here only as an interim, escapable patch – the real fix belongs on ICES’s server.

This distinction is what kept one investigation (below) from turning into an incorrect “fix.”

Fixes

1. -9 sentinel not fully scrubbed to NA

applyDatrasTypeSchema() coerced column types but never converted DATRAS’s -9 missing-value sentinel to NA. parseDatras() already caught the string "-9", but not decimal forms like "-9.0" – a valid representation DATRAS uses for missing float fields. After simplify() converts such a string to numeric, the value becomes -9 and passed through unchanged.

x <- data.frame(HaulDur = -9)
applyDatrasTypeSchema(x, record = "HH")$HaulDur
#> [1] -9      # before the fix -- should be NA

Fix: explicit -9/-9L scrubbing added to applyDatrasTypeSchema() for all int/decimal columns, after type coercion.

2. Empty or unavailable results returned FALSE/NULL instead of a data frame

getDATRAS(), getFlexFile(), getLTassessment(), getIndices(), and getCatchWgt() all had at least one path that returned a bare FALSE (an invalid survey name, an unavailable year/quarter) or, for getDATRAS(), silently returned NULL when an empty XML response collapsed via do.call(rbind, .). Both break idiomatic downstream code:

out <- getDATRAS("HH", "NS-IBTS", years = 1800, quarters = 1)
nrow(out)
#> Error: argument is not a data frame

Fix: every such early exit now returns data.frame(). getCatchWgt() needed a genuinely new guard – it has no availability checks of its own, it inherits failure from two internal getDATRAS() calls, and would otherwise hard-error on column-dependent processing against an empty result.

3. xsi:nil XML attribute leaking into column names

DATRAS represents a missing field as a self-closing tag, e.g. <Age_6 xsi:nil="true" />. parseDatras()’s name-extraction regex relied on a lazy quantifier ((.*?)) that isn’t reliably supported across regex engines, and captured the whole Age_6 xsi:nil="true" as the column name instead of Age_6.

Fix: replaced with ([^ >]+)[^>]*, which stops the capture at the first space or > without relying on lazy-quantifier support. Verified live: all 16 Age_0-Age_15 columns from a real getIndices() call now come back with clean names.

4. Literal text "NA" surviving as a real, non-missing value

A deeper, separate bug in the same area: the self-closing-tag expansion in parseDatras() produced the literal text "NA" as the field’s content, not a true NA. Two lines later, -9 and "" are explicitly normalised to NA – but "NA" was never included, and is.na("NA") is FALSE, so simplify()’s numeric-conversion guard was fooled and left the whole column as character, holding the string "NA" in every affected cell.

Fix: the tag expansion now produces empty content rather than the literal text "NA", so the existing x[x == ""] <- NA normalisation catches it – for every column type, not just numeric ones. This was a real gap beyond Age_*: declared-character columns got zero scrubbing either.

5. Field-list webserver gaps (interim patches, not code bugs)

Two corrections to getDatrasFieldList()’s existing hot-fix block, both examples of the third category above:

  • aphia naming – the hot-fix had invented aphia as the “new” name for Valid_Aphia. Cross-checked against ICES’s own getHLdataNewHeaders endpoint (the one place ICES is actively rolling out new header names) – it still calls this field Valid_Aphia, unchanged. Realigned to match ICES’s actual direction rather than this repo’s own invention.
  • CA Age gap – getDATRAS("CA", ...) returns a column literally named Age, matching neither the field list’s IndividualAge (new) nor AgeRings (old) – even with new_names = FALSE, confirming the raw server response itself uses Age. Corrected the field list’s FieldNameOld accordingly, the same pattern already used for three analogous LT corrections.

Investigated, not fixed: getCatchWgt() and DataType == "C"

The most interesting negative result. getCatchWgt() never applies a HaulDuration/60 scaling for DataType == "C" hauls – initial evidence (2020 data) showed catch weights inflated by exactly that factor on affected hauls. This looked like a clean code bug.

But R/zzz.R’s own package-startup message already warns: “there are known issues with the way CatCatchWgt has been reported until 2023.” That’s ICES’s own disclaimer, and it lines up: checking real NS-IBTS 2024 Q1 data, the median catch-per-minute-towed for DataType == "C" hauls is ~0.97x the DataType == "R" rate – not ~60x. Post-2023 submissions are already correctly per-haul.

Applying the “obvious” fix now would have broken current and future data while only helping historical records. Conclusion: a data bug, time-bounded and already resolved, not a getCatchWgt() code bug. No change made.

Branch structure

Each fix above landed on its own short-lived branch (einar_dev/sentinel-scrub, einar_dev/xsi-nil-colname-leak, einar_dev/empty-result-consistency, einar_dev/age-na-string-coercion, einar_dev/fieldlist-webserver-gaps), verified live, then merged into a single trunk, einar_dev/integration. master was left untouched throughout – deliberately, so it stays a clean, minimal-diff mirror of upstream (currently exactly one commit ahead) rather than accumulating in-progress work. The trunk is named einar_dev/integration rather than plain einar_dev for a mechanical reason: git can’t have a branch called einar_dev and branches called einar_dev/<something> coexist – the ref namespace collides – so the trunk needed its own leaf name within that namespace.

Branches were also built sequentially (each one off the latest einar_dev/integration tip, not off a shared stale point), so the result is one linear chain rather than a diverging tree. That was a deliberate choice too: three of the fixes touch R/utilities.R and two touch R/getCatchWgt.R, and building them one at a time against an up-to-date trunk avoided any multi-way merge conflicts between fixes that shared a file.

None of this branch structure is expected to matter to, or be visible to, anyone outside this fork – it’s a working method, not something upstream would ever see or need to care about.

Communication plan with ices-tools-prod

This fork and upstream are handled under deliberately different rules. The fork itself is full autonomy: push or merge here freely, no CI to wait on, no need to coordinate with anyone. Upstream is a real maintainer’s repository, shared with everyone else who depends on the package – pacing and consideration apply there, not here.

The intended loop, per bug, is:

  1. Check upstream’s existing issues first, including under this author’s own username, before filing anything new. This already paid off directly: issues #46, #47, and #48 turned out to already describe exactly what surfaced independently while building fixes 3, 4, and 5 above.
  2. File a new upstream issue before writing a fix, but only if nothing already covers it – cheap for the maintainer to read, and doesn’t block starting the fix here in parallel.
  3. Fix it here regardless of upstream’s pace, merge to this fork’s own trunk.
  4. Closing the loop upstream is a separate, later, deliberate step: a comment plus manual close on an existing issue (merging into this fork does not auto-close a different repo’s issue), or eventually an actual pull request.
  5. Sending pull requests specifically should be paced, not fired all at once, and grouped by logical fix rather than by file – fixes 3 and 4 above touch the same file but are unrelated stories and would stay separate PRs, for instance.

As of writing, nothing has been sent upstream at all: no PR opened, no issue comments posted, nothing beyond the four fixes and one investigation staying inside this fork’s own einar_dev/integration. That’s by design at this stage, not an oversight. Evidence on how upstream tends to move, gathered via the GitHub API rather than assumed: zero open PRs at the time of writing, recent (2026) PRs merged within hours to about two weeks, a few small older PRs sat roughly two months before a batch merge, and some plain issues with no PR attached have sat open for years (e.g. #26, filed 2019) – not glacially slow, but no fixed turnaround either, which is the reason for pacing deliberately rather than sending everything at once.
